This article summarizes a local benchmark run for `ahocorasick`. The benchmark
uses long English and Chinese novels as input, then compares three tasks:

- `detect`: return whether each document contains at least one pattern.
- `count`: return the total number of pattern matches per document.
- `extract`: materialize the extracted matches.

The benchmark compares `ahocorasick` with `polars`, `AhoCorasickTrie`, a basic
base R `for` loop, `tidyverse` + `stringr`, and `data.table`. Note that
`AhoCorasickTrie` is ASCII-only, so it is skipped for Chinese and mixed UTF-8
cases.

## Reproducing

The benchmark data and runners live under `bench/`. Generated output is written
to `bench/output/`, which is ignored by git.

```{bash}
#| label: run-benchmarks
#| eval: false

Rscript bench/01-generate-benchmark-data.R
Rscript bench/02-run-benchmarks.R
```

The results below come from a run with 5 iterations per expression, 200
documents per corpus, and 5000 characters per document chunk.

  | Case              | Corpus     | Patterns | Documents | Input MiB |
  | ----------------- | ---------- | -------- | --------- | --------- |
  | `en_small_common` | `en_docs`  | 32       | 200       | 0.95      |
  | `en_large_rare`   | `en_docs`  | 256      | 200       | 0.95      |
  | `zh_small_common` | `zh_docs`  | 32       | 200       | 2.82      |
  | `mix_medium`      | `mix_docs` | 64       | 200       | 1.89      |

The English corpus is built from *Crime and Punishment*, *Pride and Prejudice*,
and *The Count of Monte Cristo*. The Chinese corpus is built from `红楼梦`,
`鲁迅全集`, `三体1-3`, and `射雕英雄传`.

## Semantics

The benchmark uses fixed-string matching semantics. `ahocorasick` uses a
pre-built automaton in every timed query. `count` and `extract` use overlapping
matches.

The correctness gate checks all supported `detect` and `count` results against
`ahocorasick`. For `extract`, it checks extracted-match counts per document. All
supported methods agreed in this run.

## Build Cost

`ahocorasick` builds a reusable automaton before querying. Build time was small
for all tested pattern sets.

  | Case              | Build median ms |
  | ----------------- | --------------- |
  | `en_small_common` | 0.22            |
  | `en_large_rare`   | 0.39            |
  | `zh_small_common` | 0.24            |
  | `mix_medium`      | 0.30            |

## Detect

`ahocorasick` was the fastest method for `detect` in all four cases. The base R
loop was close for `en_small_common` because it can stop at the first common
pattern in each document. That shortcut does not hold for larger or rarer
pattern sets.

Median time in milliseconds:

  | Case              | `ahocorasick` | `polars` | `AhoCorasickTrie` | base `for` | `tidyverse` | `data.table` |
  | ----------------- | ------------- | -------- | ----------------- | ---------- | ----------- | ------------ |
  | `en_small_common` | 0.16          | 1.83     | 22.42             | 0.21       | 2.54        | 1.08         |
  | `en_large_rare`   | 0.80          | 2.61     | 5.84              | 21.59      | 25.35       | 19.29        |
  | `zh_small_common` | 0.36          | 1.94     | skipped           | 1.91       | 4.94        | 3.55         |
  | `mix_medium`      | 0.25          | 2.05     | skipped           | 1.18       | 6.34        | 4.34         |

## Count

`ahocorasick` was also the fastest method for `count` in all four cases. This is
where a reusable automaton matters most: repeated fixed-string scans have to
scan the documents once per pattern, while Aho-Corasick can scan once for the
whole pattern set.

Median time in milliseconds:

  | Case              | `ahocorasick` | `polars` | `AhoCorasickTrie` | base `for` | `tidyverse` | `data.table` |
  | ----------------- | ------------- | -------- | ----------------- | ---------- | ----------- | ------------ |
  | `en_small_common` | 2.49          | 27.77    | 21.51             | 22.99      | 5.95        | 4.58         |
  | `en_large_rare`   | 2.04          | 223.34   | 5.53              | 169.39     | 25.44       | 18.69        |
  | `zh_small_common` | 5.84          | 37.11    | skipped           | 81.88      | 12.47       | 10.67        |
  | `mix_medium`      | 3.41          | 55.26    | skipped           | 109.44     | 12.91       | 9.43         |

## Extract

`extract` measures the cost of materializing match results, not just searching.
`ahocorasick::ac_extract_df()` is the fastest method in all four cases. It
returns a long data frame directly from the Rust output, avoiding the overhead
in R.

Median time in milliseconds:

  | Case              | `ahocorasick` | `polars` | `AhoCorasickTrie` | base `for` | `tidyverse` | `data.table` |
  | ----------------- | ------------- | -------- | ----------------- | ---------- | ----------- | ------------ |
  | `en_small_common` | 7.30          | 9.92     | 21.54             | 930.72     | 790.93      | 790.69       |
  | `en_large_rare`   | 2.33          | 4.11     | 5.13              | 302.23     | 147.84      | 151.74       |
  | `zh_small_common` | 7.61          | 9.33     | skipped           | 1072.92    | 569.07      | 608.51       |
  | `mix_medium`      | 7.01          | 9.05     | skipped           | 1675.84    | 1143.16     | 1172.35      |

## Summary

Use `ahocorasick` when you need fast reusable multi-pattern matching over R
character vectors, especially with UTF-8 text. In this run it is consistently
fastest for `detect`, `count`, and `extract`.

Use `polars` if your data is already in a DataFrame and you want to both keep in
the DataFrame workflow and have good performance. Try it!
